claims.plain: Being the one who decides makes participants less happy, whatever the outcome turns out to be.
Deciding on another person's behalf is unpleasant in itself, whether or not the partner comes to harm.
The unhappiness after a partner's loss comes from the participant's own bad outcome, not from guilt about the partner.
The imaging pipeline does not recover effects that are already established, so its condition differences mean nothing.
The model-based fMRI analysis does not recover known brain signals, so its partner reward-surprise regressors cannot be trusted.
Participants chose inattentively or at random, so their choices carry no information about what they preferred or felt.
Choosing on someone else's behalf simply changes how much risk a person will accept, and that is what the differences reflect.
The drop in happiness after a partner's loss appears whether or not the participant won their own lottery.
Participants become less happy after a partner's bad outcome when they made the choice than when the partner did.
How closely a participant's brain response matches the published guilt signature does not predict their behavioural guilt effect.
Participants' moment-to-moment happiness rises with their own winnings and also with their partner's.
Anterior insula carries interpersonal guilt, responding when the participant's own choice is what harmed the partner.
A partner's unexpectedly bad outcomes lower a participant's happiness in their own right when the participant's choice caused them.
Superior temporal sulcus represents what the partner is feeling only when the participant is responsible for the partner's outcome.
The anterior insula guilt response matches the published Yu and Koban brain signature of guilt.
Anterior insula and inferior frontal gyrus are more strongly coupled when the participant is the one choosing for the partner.
The anterior insula responds more when a partner loses because of the participant's choice.
Yu and Koban derived a whole-brain activity pattern that identifies guilt across paradigms, weighted most heavily on anterior insula.
Participants chose the lottery more often the more it was worth, in both studies.
The partner was an expected-value-maximising algorithm rather than a person, and participants were never told so.
Precuneus, left temporoparietal junction and medial prefrontal cortex respond more when deciding for a partner than for oneself alone.
Happiness should fall further after a partner's bad outcome when the participant chose than when the partner chose.
Anterior insula should respond more when the participant chose than when the partner chose, after partner losses but not partner wins.
A happiness model that gives its own weight to partner losses the participant caused should fit the ratings better than models without one.
Left superior temporal sulcus should track partner reward surprises on participant-chosen trials but not on partner-chosen ones.
A happiness model with a responsibility term accounts for the guilt effect better than models without one.
Risk premiums were no different when participants chose for a partner than when they chose for themselves alone, in either study.
All findings come from two studies, an fMRI study and a behavioural replication, using the same lottery task with an algorithmic partner.
Partner reward surprises that the participant's own choice produced carry their own weight in happiness, in both studies.

claims.plain: Participants took the lottery slightly more often when choosing for themselves alone in the first study, but not in the second.
Superior temporal sulcus tracks surprises in the partner's reward only when the participant made the choice.
Ventral striatum on both sides responds more the larger the reward the computational model expects.
Ventral striatum responds more when participants take the risky lottery rather than the safe option, whoever they are choosing for.
